content: Copper deficiency in humans or other mammals can lead to a syndrome characterized by anemia or pancytopenia, as well as neurodegeneration. In ruminant animals, the neurodegenerative syndrome associated with copper deficiency has been recognized for a long time and is commonly referred to as swayback. These animals typically develop symptoms such as ataxia and spasticity. In humans, cases of anemia caused by copper deficiency are rare but have been documented for many years. More recently, a syndrome resembling ruminant swayback has been observed in humans. Individuals affected by this condition may experience progressive spasticity, ataxia, and neuropathy. This neurological presentation may also be accompanied by anemia. The clinical manifestations of copper deficiency in humans closely resemble those of subacute combined degeneration, a well-known condition caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. In ruminants, copper deficiency is often due to grazing on copper-deficient lands or consuming feed that lacks adequate copper. In humans, copper deficiency can result from copper-deficient parenteral nutrition or as a consequence of gastric bypass surgery. The recommended daily intake of elemental copper for an adult is 0.9 mg. However, typical American diets may not provide sufficient copper. Additionally, zinc competes with copper for absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Chronic excessive zinc intake, such as that seen in individuals who overuse denture adhesive products containing zinc, can lead to copper deficiency.
